title: Use of alcohol protective behavioral strategies among college students: A critical review

claims.statement: In college students, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), evidence is insufficient to say whether using more protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver), compared with using fewer, lowers drinking or alcohol-related problems. Students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. Asked how often they used strategies when they drank, students who reported more said they drank less (negative correlations in three studies in one paper by the author's team), and in three studies students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems; the review gives the size of almost none of these links. Over time the links were weaker or mixed: in one study 3 of 9 correlations with later problems were not significant; in another, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; in women, strategies reported at the start went with fewer problems 4 months later but not with drinking at the same time. In two studies of day-by-day reports (one a 15-day diary of 40 students), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, part of the fall in drinking or problems was statistically explained by a rise in reported strategy use (mediation); in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: No pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: negative correlations with drinking in 3 studies using a how-often-when-drinking scale, and positive ones with a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions; a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant (1 study); day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).
